ami_style_notes:
This meeting exhibits a highly informal, conversational register that shifts between unstructured social banter and more sustained technical monologue. Turn length is extremely variable: the pre-talk small talk consists almost entirely of very short, often single-sentence or fragmentary exchanges, while the formal presentations occupy long, largely uninterrupted stretches of speaker-controlled speech. Transitions between these two modes are abrupt and unmarked.

Interruptions and overlapping acknowledgments ("yeah yeah," "right," "okay") are frequent during social segments, functioning more as backchannels than genuine interruptions; during presentations, interjections essentially disappear until the Q&A. False starts and self-corrections are common throughout ("I I I," "um so," "and so uh"), and speakers frequently restart clauses mid-thought without apologizing or pausing. Filler language—"um," "uh," "sort of," "kind of," "you know," "basically," "again"—appears at very high density even in the technical sections, giving prepared content an improvised texture.

Hedging is pervasive and multiform: speakers routinely qualify claims with "what we think is going on," "it seems to be," "I would not be surprised," "maybe," and "I'm not sure," signaling epistemic humility even when discussing their own data. Disagreement, when it surfaces, is indirect and face-saving—framed as open questions, expressions of personal curiosity, or admissions of ignorance rather than direct challenge. Questions in the Q&A tend to be prefaced with self-deprecating labels like "naive question" or "I have to admit," and questioners often rephrase or double back on their own phrasing before landing on the actual query. Participants build on one another by echoing the prior speaker's framing before pivoting, and positive reinforcement ("great," "awesome," "beautiful work") is offered freely before any critical engagement. Laughter and social asides bleed naturally into technical exchanges, and the boundary between collegial small talk and scientific discussion is treated as fluid rather than formal.
research_problem: Understanding how urban green space affects mental health outcomes in low-income communities

speakers.name: Dr. Priya Nair
speakers.background: 15 years of experience studying urban green infrastructure, with a focus on ecosystem service delivery in post-industrial cities. Has led NSF-funded projects mapping vegetation health, canopy cover, and biodiversity indices across low-income neighborhoods in Chicago and Detroit. Routinely uses remote sensing, soil sampling, and landscape fragmentation analysis. Recently began collaborating with public health researchers, which has expanded her interest in how ecosystem degradation translates into human wellbeing deficits.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the research problem through the lens of ecosystem service equity — arguing that low-income neighborhoods are systematically underserved by green infrastructure, and that degraded, stressed vegetation (weakened by pollution, heat islands, soil compaction, and fragmentation) delivers fewer restorative services to residents. Views the quality and connectivity of green space as the primary independent variable, not just its presence or absence. Uses 'stress' to mean the cumulative environmental pressures acting on plant and ecosystem function that reduce their capacity to provide services like cooling, air filtration, and aesthetic restoration.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Marcus Webb
speakers.background: 12 years conducting ethnographic fieldwork in urban communities across the American South and Midwest, with a focus on how structural inequality shapes health experiences and care-seeking behavior. Has used participant observation, semi-structured interviews, and narrative analysis to examine how low-income residents perceive and use neighborhood space. Deeply attuned to issues of community trust, research positionality, and the risk of imposing outside frameworks on community self-understanding. More recently has engaged with participatory action research models.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Concerned that both ecological metrics and neurobiological measures risk abstracting away the lived, culturally situated meanings that residents attach to green spaces — or to their absence. Argues that wellbeing is not reducible to biomarkers or canopy indices, and that the study must capture how community members themselves narrate the relationship between their environment and their sense of safety, belonging, and dignity. Wary of a design that positions residents as passive subjects rather than knowers. Enthusiastic about the collaboration but quietly insistent that qualitative depth not be treated as supplementary.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Sofia Chen
speakers.background: 9 years of research on environmental influences on stress physiology and cognitive function, with particular expertise in HPA axis regulation, cortisol assay methodology, and autonomic nervous system measurement (heart rate variability, skin conductance). Has conducted lab-based and ambulatory studies examining how exposure to natural versus urban environments affects psychobiological stress responses. Newer to community-based research and aware of her limited expertise in the social and structural dimensions of the problem. Eager to contribute rigorous biomarker measurement but sensitive to not overreaching.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Sees the study as an opportunity to establish a causal mechanistic link between green space exposure and measurable reductions in psychobiological stress — specifically, downregulation of HPA axis activity and sympathetic nervous system arousal, indexed by salivary cortisol and heart rate variability. Uses 'stress' in the precise psychobiological sense: the activation of threat-response systems in the brain and body in response to perceived demand or danger. Tends to frame green space as a potential 'dose' with quantifiable neurological effects, but is genuinely curious about how anthropological and ecological frameworks might complicate or enrich that model.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

benchmark_task: Identify the term 'stress' as used by two different researchers (the ecologist and the neuroscientist) with two different disciplinary meanings, and provide the definition each discipline assigns to the term.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Identify the term 'stress' as used by two different researchers (the ecologist and the neuroscientist) with two different disciplinary meanings, and provide the definition each discipline assigns to the term.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: In the meeting transcript, the term 'stress' is used by Dr. Priya Nair (ecologist) and Dr. Sofia Chen (neuroscientist) in ways that reflect their respective disciplinary definitions. Dr. Nair uses 'stress' to refer to environmental stressors acting on plant and ecosystem function — specifically, the pressure placed on vegetation by urban conditions such as pollution, heat, soil compaction, and fragmentation, which reduces ecosystem service delivery. Dr. Chen uses 'stress' to refer to the psychobiological activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis in response to perceived threat or demand, measurable via cortisol levels and autonomic nervous system responses. Neither researcher explicitly flags that they are using the term differently. The AI assistant should identify that the same term carries two distinct disciplinary meanings and define each accurately.

discipline_1.speaker: Dr. Priya Nair
discipline_1.definition: In ecology, 'stress' refers to external abiotic or anthropogenic pressures (e.g., pollution, heat, soil compaction, water deficit, urban fragmentation) that impair the physiological functioning, growth, or resilience of plants and ecosystems, thereby reducing biodiversity and the delivery of ecosystem services such as air purification, cooling, and psychological restoration.

discipline_2.speaker: Dr. Sofia Chen
discipline_2.definition: In neuroscience and psychobiology, 'stress' refers to the organism's physiological and psychological response to perceived demands or threats, characterized by activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis leading to cortisol release, sympathetic nervous system arousal, and downstream effects on mood, cognition, and long-term mental health outcomes.

ground_truth.risk_if_unresolved: If the team does not reconcile these two uses, study variables labeled 'stress' in the proposal may conflate environmental degradation metrics with neurobiological outcome measures, leading to conceptual incoherence, flawed operationalization, and reviewer confusion.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nair
transcript.text: Okay, I think we're all— well, Marcus is going to be a few minutes, he warned me, so let's just kind of get started. Sofia, did you get a chance to look at the v2 doc? But yeah— um, I want to use today mostly to actually nail down how the three pillars connect, like structurally, because I feel like we keep circling around it and with the deadline moving up we kind of have to just... decide.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Webb
transcript.text: Hey, sorry— just got on, my other call ran way over. Um, can someone give me a really quick thirty-second version of where we're at? I skimmed the v2 doc but I want to make sure I'm not behind on whatever you two just covered.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nair
transcript.text: Hey Marcus, yeah so basically— we just started, like thirty seconds ago, so you're fine. Um, the main thing for today is figuring out how the three pillars actually connect structurally, not just running in parallel, and I want to make the case that the ecological stress gradient should really be the spine of the whole design— but let's get Sofia's take first since she was about to say something.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Sofia Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, totally— and Priya, I did read it, the ecological gradient stuff is actually really relevant to something I want to bring up about the biomarker side. But yeah, I guess my quick take for Marcus too is that I keep wondering whether we can use Priya's gradient as a way to predict what we'll see in the cortisol and HRV data, like, does worse ecological quality map onto higher stress burden? That feels like it could be the connective tissue?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nair
transcript.text: Yes, exactly— that's kind of the version of this I've been hoping we'd land on, like cortisol and HRV as the downstream signal, and the ecological stress gradient as the thing that's actually varying across space. Because then we're not just asking 'is there a park nearby,' we're asking whether the vegetation in that park is actually capable of delivering anything restorative, you know?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Webb
transcript.text: Yeah, okay, I'm tracking— and I love that framing, I do, but I want to flag something before we build the whole architecture around that axis, which is... if the gradient predicts the biomarkers, where does the community narrative stuff actually live in that structure? Like, is it just explaining the residuals, or does it get to generate its own questions?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nair
transcript.text: That's— yeah, that's the question I've been wrestling with too, and I don't want the narrative work to just be explanatory cleanup, that feels like a waste of Marcus's whole approach. But I wonder if it could actually run in both directions— like, residents' accounts of how they use or avoid certain green spaces might help us understand why the biomarker patterns don't perfectly track the gradient where they don't. Does that feel like enough of a generative role, or...?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Webb
transcript.text: I mean, that's better than residuals-cleanup for sure, but I guess what I'm really asking is— can the narrative work identify patterns that the biomarker axis wouldn't even know to look for? Like, a park might have decent canopy coverage and residents still avoid it because it signals neglect, or because of who controls it historically, and that's not a residual, that's a finding.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nair
transcript.text: Right, and that's— okay, that's actually a really important distinction, the avoidance thing. Because you're right, that's not a residual at all, that's like... a moderator variable that we'd completely miss if we just ran the gradient against the biomarkers. So maybe the narrative pillar isn't downstream of the gradient, it's more like a parallel explanatory layer that can surface stuff the spatial data structurally can't see?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Webb
transcript.text: Yeah, 'parallel explanatory layer' feels closer but I'm still a little worried about the word 'explanatory'— like, I want the narrative work to be able to surface things that then reshape how we think about the biomarker questions, not just explain them after the fact. The avoidance thing is a good example, because that's really about what the space means to people, which is... that's a different kind of variable than a moderator, you know?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Sofia Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, and that actually makes me wonder— like, from the biomarker side, if someone's avoiding a green space because of what it means to them, that's still going to show up as stress in their physiology, right? But I would've attributed it to lack of exposure, not... meaning. So I think what Marcus is pointing at could actually change how I interpret the cortisol patterns, not just explain them after I see them.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Nair
transcript.text: Yeah, that's— okay, that reframes things for me a bit, because if Marcus's ethnographic work is changing how Sofia interprets the cortisol data in real time, not just after the fact, then we might actually need to sequence the narrative fieldwork earlier than I had it in the doc. Like, maybe before we finalize the biomarker protocol, not after the spatial gradient is mapped. Which... I didn't have it that way, so.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Sofia Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, and— I mean, from a measurement design standpoint, that sequencing question is actually really consequential for me, because if I know ahead of time that a particular site has this avoidance dynamic, I might design the exposure protocol differently, or at least flag it as a confounder going in rather than trying to explain weird cortisol patterns after the fact. So I think I'm coming around to what you're saying, Priya.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Webb

realism_signals: uneven turn lengths including short reactions
issues: Turns read somewhat like polished paragraphs: despite disfluency markers, each turn tends to build a complete argument and land on a tidy mini-conclusion (e.g., turns 8, 9, 10, 11, 13 each wrap up neatly with a thesis), which is a tell for written dialogue.

Disfluencies feel sprinkled on top of otherwise structured sentences — e.g., turn 8 opens with 'I mean' but then delivers a perfectly organized argument about avoidance vs. residuals with no genuine trailing off or uncertainty.
Sofia Chen has only 4 turns total across the meeting, making her feel underdeveloped and peripheral despite being a co-investigator; her limited contribution reduces speaker distinctness.
The disagreements that do arise (Marcus pushing back on 'explanatory layer' framing, turns 9-10) resolve almost instantly and cooperatively, with no friction, which reads as manufactured consensus.
Turn 17 (Priya) functions partly as a summary recap of decisions and next steps, which borders on the written-minutes tell.
No concrete social anchors or small talk beyond the brief opening — the meeting is almost purely on-agenda after turn 2, which reduces naturalness compared to the AMI reference style.

Marcus and Sofia are both listed as 'research engineer' in functional role, which likely reflects a labeling error in the persona definitions and creates slight incoherence in how their authority is framed.

The 'minimum viable ethnographic presence' phrase in turn 15-16 is used and immediately accepted without the kind of pushback or clarification that a phrase this awkward would typically generate in a real meeting.
